title: Filibuster

jokes.text: Andy sings a custom song about coming home from London: 'Someone's back from London / No, it's not the Queen / Someone's back from London / It's not Mr. Bean / It's not the royal baby / I think his name is Jeff'
jokes.setup: April appears to be preparing for a Skype date with Andy, who is in London
jokes.punchline: Andy bursts in singing a goofy self-composed song, culminating in the absurd non-sequitur 'I think his name is Jeff' referencing the royal baby
jokes.explanation: The song is perfectly Andy — childlike, joyful, and completely unself-conscious. 'I think his name is Jeff' is a delightful absurdist non-sequitur about the royal baby that feels entirely specific to Andy's character. The setup (April expecting Skype) makes the physical surprise land even harder.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You look lovely.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm going to kill you.

jokes.text: Andy: 'You're never going to need that computer again.' Beat. 'Because I'm home for, like, nineteen hours.'
jokes.setup: Andy declares April will never need the computer again, implying he's home permanently
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts the romantic gesture: he's only home for nineteen hours
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect comedic structure. The pause between the grand romantic statement and the immediate qualifier is expertly timed. It's deeply character-specific to Andy — he means well, he's trying to be romantic, but he bungles the delivery in a way that's entirely true to him. Strong economy and a genuine earned laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: She's back from London, she's back from London, she's back from London!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Is it the Queen? No. Is it Big Ben? No. Is it the royal baby? Maybe! I think his name is Jeff.

jokes.text: Andy tells Jerry 'Take a hike, Jerry.' Jerry corrects him: 'It's Larry now.' Andy: 'Okay. Take a hike, Larry.'
jokes.setup: Andy dismisses the bystander in the middle of his reunion with April, calling him by the wrong name
jokes.punchline: After being corrected to 'Larry,' Andy simply repeats the dismissal with equal indifference — the name correction changes nothing
jokes.explanation: A tight, well-executed entry in the Jerry/Gary/Larry running gag. The beat works because it takes the gag's premise — nobody respects Jerry enough to learn his name — and adds a new dimension: even when corrected, the disrespect is unchanged. Economical and effective.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Get out of here, Gary.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: It's actually Larry.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I don't care, Larry. Get out.

jokes.text: Councilman Jamm addresses Ben: 'That's right, Stretch. And looking mighty fly in that suit, brother.'
jokes.setup: Jamm is about to introduce a voter-suppression bill
jokes.punchline: He opens with bizarrely forced, tone-deaf slang ('mighty fly,' 'brother') directed at the lanky, awkward Ben
jokes.explanation: Jamm's cringe-worthy social obliviousness is a reliable character note. The joke works on Jamm's character — he's trying to be affable and comes off as deeply weird — but it's not a standout execution of the bit.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: He tried to spread rumors that my real name is Leslie Knope-Sistine, which is both absurdly specific and offensive to the Sistine Chapel.

jokes.text: Leslie talking-head: 'Last week, he tried to have me listed on the ballot as Leslie Buttface Hitler the Fourth.'
jokes.setup: Leslie describes Jamm's ongoing attempts to undermine her in the recall election
jokes.punchline: The ballot name is absurdly specific — not just an insult, but a generational insult, implying there were three previous Leslie Buttface Hitlers
jokes.explanation: The 'the Fourth' is the key comedic detail — it transforms a generic insult into something brilliantly specific and absurd. It implies a lineage, a dynasty of Leslie Buttface Hitlers, which is the kind of escalation detail that separates good joke writers from great ones. High quotability, strong originality for a line this short.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I second Leslie's motion.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And I want to be clear that my support is based purely on the merits of the proposal and has nothing to do with the fact that I find Leslie's passion for civic engagement deeply attractive, or that I've noticed she smells like coconut and ambition, or that I would very much like to take her to dinner at that Italian place downtown, or—

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head after the vote: 'I just get excited when you like me.'
jokes.setup: Ben seconds Leslie's motion to table Jamm's bill; Leslie thanks him warmly
jokes.punchline: Her aside reveals an almost childlike emotional transparency — she's genuinely thrilled her husband supported her in a work setting
jokes.explanation: A sweet, character-specific moment that gets a warm laugh. It's totally Leslie — earnest, emotionally unguarded, and slightly absurd in a professional context. Not a huge laugh but very on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Give me those votes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Give me those votes!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: GIVE ME THOSE VOTES!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I don't have any votes. They're in a database.

jokes.text: Ben talking-head about roller skating: 'I have a thing for women in skates, okay? Everyone has a thing, and that's mine. As far as things go, it's pretty innocuous. I could be one of those dudes that kisses mannequins or whatever.'
jokes.setup: Ben explains why he requested a roller skating birthday party
jokes.punchline: He defensively normalizes his harmless kink by comparing it to mannequin-kissing, which is delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Ben's talking-head confessional is character-perfect: the escalating self-justification, the specific and bizarre comparison case ('dudes that kisses mannequins'), and the follow-up beat where he stares longingly. The structure of 'I could be worse' as a defense is well-executed and specific to Ben's anxious self-awareness.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's innocuous. I mean, some people kiss mannequins.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm attracted to women on roller skates. A lot.

jokes.text: April's '90s party outfit gets criticized: 'Hey, Ann. Ann called. She wants her ugly outfit back.'
jokes.setup: April arrives at the party dressed in '90s fashion
jokes.punchline: The insult is framed as a message from Ann — a callback to the classic 'called, wants their [thing] back' format — implying Ann would wear something this ugly
jokes.explanation: A functional but generic insult joke using an overused format. It gets a mild chuckle but doesn't do anything interesting with the Ann/April dynamic or the '90s theme. Competent filler.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann's outfit called. It wants to be attractive again.

jokes.text: Donna dressed as a pilgrim at the '90s party. Someone asks why; she says: 'Leslie said it was a Come As You Were in the Nineties party. I assumed it was the 1690s.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is dressed in early '90s fashion for the party
jokes.punchline: Donna interpreted 'the Nineties' as the 1690s and dressed as a pilgrim, delivered with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: A clean, well-structured visual/dialogue joke. Donna dressed as a pilgrim at a '90s party is inherently funny, and her deadpan explanation makes it better. The follow-up ('we'd all be mummies') adds a second laugh beat efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I interpreted '90s as 1690s instead of 1990s.

jokes.text: Someone corrects Donna: 'Babe, if it was the 1690s, we'd all be mummies.' Donna: 'What do you think mummies are? Skeletons?' Someone: 'Oh, boy.'
jokes.setup: The 1690s pilgrim joke leads to a correction about what would happen if the party were set in 1690
jokes.punchline: Donna's serious, earnest confusion about mummies vs. skeletons suggests she believes mummies are simply dead people from that era — a delightful non-sequitur of ignorance
jokes.explanation: The escalation from the pilgrim gag into genuine confusion about what constitutes a mummy is a great extension. Donna's sincere 'What do you think mummies are? Skeletons?' treats her misconception as a reasonable question, which is the source of the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, mummies aren't skeletons. Mummies are wrapped up dead bodies.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I know that.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Then why are you dressed as a skeleton?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Because that's what mummies are.

jokes.text: Tom greets someone in backwards pants: 'You look wiggity, wiggity, wiggity, wiggity wonderful.' Then identifies it: 'Wait a minute. Pants on backwards. Kris Kross, right?'
jokes.setup: A partygoer arrives in '90s-themed costume
jokes.punchline: Tom enthusiastically deploys a Kris Kross reference, seamlessly blending the compliment with the identification — he's completely in his element
jokes.explanation: Classic Tom: effortlessly pop-culture fluent, enthusiastic, a little show-offy. The 'wiggity wiggity' phrasing is perfectly character-specific — Tom would absolutely know this and deploy it instantly. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Well, you have to take off your shoes, then your socks, then your pants, then your underwear. It's a real nightmare.

jokes.text: Backwards-pants guy admits: 'I actually just went. I had to pull my pants all the way to the ground like a toddler.'
jokes.setup: Tom asks what happens when you have to pee with backwards Kris Kross pants
jokes.punchline: The person confirms they already dealt with it — and had to fully drop their pants to the ground like a toddler
jokes.explanation: The callback works well — Tom's practical question gets a practical, undignified answer. 'Like a toddler' is the precise detail that elevates it from a simple acknowledgment to a proper punchline. Good structure, decent laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Nadia is completely out of my league. I mean, she's like the NBA and I'm like a muffler store worker. She's dunking on people, making millions of dollars, and I'm like, 'Your muffler's draggin', buddy.'

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head about Nadia: 'She's definitely out of my league. Actually, we're not even playing the same sport. It's kind of like she's in the NBA, and I work in a muffler store next to the stadium.'
jokes.setup: Tom introduces Nadia as a super-hot doctor who's been hanging out with him
jokes.punchline: The league metaphor escalates from 'different league' to 'different sport' to 'muffler store next to the stadium' — each step more self-deprecating and specific
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional joke construction. The three-step escalation — 'out of my league' → 'not even the same sport' → 'muffler store next to the stadium' — is a masterclass in comedic specificity. The muffler store detail is the precise, unexpected image that makes the joke memorable and highly quotable. Strong candidate for the episode's best line.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.line: I'm doing humanitarian work in Rwanda.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, that sounds like a stupid vacation.

jokes.text: Tom's friend dismisses Doctors Without Borders as 'a stupid vacation.' Tom: 'Exactly.'
jokes.setup: Tom complains they just met and she has to leave; she explains she's going to Rwanda with Doctors Without Borders
jokes.punchline: Tom's friend dismisses one of the most selfless humanitarian missions as 'a stupid vacation,' and Tom immediately agrees
jokes.explanation: The joke works on the absurdist logic of Tom's self-centered worldview — of course Doctors Without Borders is a 'stupid vacation' from the perspective of someone who just wants to keep dating her. The instantaneous 'Exactly' from Tom is economical and character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, I didn't want to be another Indian guy who went pro in skee ball. That's like the most clichéd thing ever.

jokes.text: Tom brags about being a skee ball master. Nadia: 'No way. Why didn't you go pro?' Tom: 'Hmm. I don't know. I didn't want to be a cliché. Yet another professional Indian skee ball player.'
jokes.setup: Tom claims to be a skee ball master; Nadia playfully asks why he didn't go pro
jokes.punchline: Tom's self-deprecating answer subverts the setup by acknowledging that 'professional Indian skee ball player' is so far from a cliché it's absurd
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sharp joke. Tom uses self-deprecating racial humor in a way that's entirely specific to his character — the joke isn't about stereotypes, it's about the total absence of any stereotype, making the 'cliché' framing absurd. Aziz Ansari's delivery would be perfect here. High originality, strong structure, character-specific. One of the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: So the point of the game is to shoot the ducks?

jokes.text: Ron confidently offers Donna hunting tips before an arcade shooting game, declaring 'Hunting, Donna, is about silence, balance, and patience.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Donna approach an arcade hunting video game
jokes.punchline: Ron pompously applies real-world hunting philosophy to an arcade game, setting up his imminent failure
jokes.explanation: The setup is classic Ron — he cannot encounter anything without asserting mastery. The comedy comes from knowing he's about to be humiliated by a children's arcade game. Strong character integration; Ron's philosophical delivery of hunting wisdom to a Chuck E. Cheese-style game is inherently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: This game is wildly inaccurate. The recoil is all wrong, and no self-respecting elk would stand still for this long.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Can I have my money back?

jokes.text: Ron completely misses every deer on the arcade hunting game. Donna: 'Hey, you know you're supposed to hit the deer, right?'
jokes.setup: Ron has just pompously explained hunting philosophy and stepped up to the game
jokes.punchline: Ron shoots wildly and misses everything, requiring Donna to point out the basic objective
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Ron's pompous setup lands well. The visual comedy of Ron — a man who treats hunting as sacred — failing spectacularly at an arcade hunting game is inherently funny. Donna's deadpan correction is perfectly economical.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not a sore loser.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A sore loser is someone who, when faced with a loss, makes excuses, blames others, and refuses to acknowledge their opponent's superior play.

jokes.text: Donna (to Ron after he's losing): 'Get it together, Swanson.'
jokes.setup: Ron is supposed to be the expert hunter but is clearly losing to Donna at the arcade game.
jokes.punchline: Donna's terse, casual dressing-down of Ron — using his last name like a coach — inverts the power dynamic established in his condescending 'pointers' offer.
jokes.explanation: A clean, economical payoff to the setup of Ron offering condescending pointers. Donna calling him 'Swanson' is a nice power-reversal detail. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so in London, they have this word... 'brilliant.' It means really good.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's just... a regular word.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, but they say it all the time. It's like they invented it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We use that word here.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Not like this. In London, everything is 'brilliant.' The weather? Brilliant. A cup of tea? Brilliant. A stabbing? Brilliant.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head after losing: 'Get it together, Swanson.' Then rationalizes: 'The game is absurd. This gun is lightweight, there's no sight, and we are far too close to these deer. Would they not smell us?'
jokes.setup: Ron has just been humiliated by an arcade game
jokes.punchline: Rather than accepting he lost, Ron delivers a detailed technical critique of the game's unrealism as if it were a genuine hunting deficiency
jokes.explanation: 'Would they not smell us?' is the line that elevates this from a standard sore-loser joke to something exceptional. Ron's brain genuinely cannot process a game loss — his only recourse is to critique the game's hunting authenticity with dead seriousness. The self-admonishment 'Get it together, Swanson' before the rationalization is a perfect comedic structure. Very strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm like Chuck Norris, but with paperwork.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I want my money back. How do I get my quarters?'
jokes.setup: Ron has just delivered a detailed critique of the arcade game's unrealism
jokes.punchline: He concludes by demanding a refund, as if the game's unrealism constitutes grounds for consumer complaint
jokes.explanation: A tight button to the arcade game sequence. Ron's indignation translating into a formal refund request is economical and on-brand. Works as a closer to the sequence without overextending.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Making out is like karate. You gotta know when to strike, when to pull back, when to make that 'HIIII-YAH!' sound.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You just made that sound while kissing me.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know. It really adds to it.

jokes.text: Donna: 'Oh, my God! You are such a sore loser.' Ron: 'I am not a sore loser. It's just that I prefer to win. And when I don't, I get furious. Employee!'
jokes.setup: Donna calls Ron a sore loser
jokes.punchline: Ron's denial is immediately undercut by a perfect definition of sore losing ('I prefer to win. And when I don't, I get furious.') followed by the non-sequitur 'Employee!' — suggesting he's about to escalate to management
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'I am not a sore loser. It's just that I prefer to win. And when I don't, I get furious.' is a textbook example of a character defining themselves through self-contradiction while being completely earnest. The 'Employee!' button is perfect — Ron would absolutely escalate a children's arcade game loss to staff. High quotability, excellent structure. Comparable to anchor examples.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Why would you play 'Automatic for the People' at an early '90s party? That album came out in '92.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, it's a great album.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm not saying it's not great. I'm saying if you're doing an early '90s party, you need 'Out of Time' from '91. You can't just throw any REM album at people and call it a theme.

jokes.text: Andy describes his London work: 'I'm like Chuck Norris. Only instead of crushing bad guys' skulls, I'm crushing documents.'
jokes.setup: April asks Andy about work in London; he says he's kicking ass
jokes.punchline: The Chuck Norris comparison deflates immediately when the 'crushing' is applied to paperwork
jokes.explanation: A solid Andy joke — he genuinely believes the Chuck Norris comparison applies to document management, which reveals both his enthusiasm and his obliviousness. Gets a good laugh and sets up the later callback beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: That's like my pants when I saw a stripper named Candy in Atlantic City.

jokes.text: April to Andy: 'Now, be the Chuck Norris of making out with me. I'll karate punch your face with my tongue. Prove it. Hi-ya.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just used a Chuck Norris metaphor for his work
jokes.punchline: April immediately appropriates the metaphor for a make-out session, culminating in 'I'll karate punch your face with my tongue' — a deeply strange and specific image
jokes.explanation: 'I'll karate punch your face with my tongue' is one of the episode's more absurdist and memorable lines — it's disgusting and romantic in equal measure, and completely specific to April and Andy's dynamic. The 'Hi-ya' button is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie's going to filibuster in roller skates. This is... this is sexually exciting for me given my skate fetish.

jokes.text: Ben's talking-head about the DJ: 'I just asked the DJ what REM albums he has. He's got Monster, but not Automatic for the People.' April: 'Wow.' Ben: 'I know. It's like, what is this, a mid-'90s party? No, it's an early '90s party.'
jokes.setup: Ben is very invested in the early '90s theme of his birthday party
jokes.punchline: The distinction between 'Monster' (1994) and 'Automatic for the People' (1992) as a meaningful party integrity issue is treated with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: This joke works on multiple levels: it's extremely specific (requiring knowledge of REM's discography), it's deeply character-specific to Ben's nerdy '90s obsession, and it treats an absurdly minor distinction as a genuine crisis. The 'Wow' / 'I know' exchange with April sells it perfectly — she's matching his energy unironically.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, you were supposed to be watching for security!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I was watching. I watched the whole thing. It was hilarious.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You let me get caught on purpose?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Tom, I'm not gonna lie to you, that was the most entertainment I've had all week.

jokes.text: Leslie practicing a synchronized couples' skate to 'Losing My Religion' while Larry/Jerry watches and evaluates
jokes.setup: Leslie is hosting Ben's birthday party; they ask Larry to watch their couples' skate routine
jokes.punchline: The specific song choice ('Losing My Religion') for a romantic birthday couples' skate and the formal choreography practice is inherently absurd
jokes.explanation: The visual of Leslie and Ben practicing a synchronized couples' skate to a breakup-adjacent REM song is funny and very Ben. Not the strongest joke but contributes to the party atmosphere and Ben's character. The interruption that follows makes this setup pay off.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: When I was eight years old, I organized a neighborhood election for class president. I had campaign signs, I did door-to-door canvassing, I had a whole platform. And when I lost, I demanded a recount. My opponent was my best friend Jennifer, and I'm pretty sure her mom bought votes with Capri Suns.

jokes.text: Jamm arrives at the skating rink to call a special session, sees Leslie in roller skates: 'What is up with the roller skates?' Leslie explains she was about to attend a birthday party. Jamm: 'Yeah, I don't care. I'm a blades guy.'
jokes.setup: Jamm interrupts the birthday party with an emergency council session; Leslie is still in roller skates
jokes.punchline: After Leslie explains herself, Jamm dismisses it with 'I'm a blades guy' — a completely irrelevant personal preference that clarifies nothing and establishes his total self-absorption
jokes.explanation: 'I'm a blades guy' is a perfect Jamm line — utterly irrelevant, self-absorbed, and delivered as if it's a meaningful statement. It reveals that he processed Leslie's explanation solely through the lens of his own skating preferences. Very economical and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, how long have I been talking?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Eight minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Eight minutes?! It felt like hours!

jokes.text: Jamm's reaction to Leslie announcing a filibuster: 'A filibuster? Are you dooking on my chest right now?'
jokes.setup: Leslie announces she will filibuster rather than yield
jokes.punchline: 'Dooking' is an invented/slang term for defecating, used as an expression of disbelief — Jamm's profane surprise is filtered through his peculiar vocabulary
jokes.explanation: 'Dooking' is a Jamm-specific profanity substitute that's disgusting and memorable. It captures his character perfectly — crude but also strangely specific. Not a huge laugh but a solid Jamm moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: This is actually... kind of amazing. Leslie, you're doing great.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I can't believe I'm saying this, but watching you navigate parliamentary procedure is legitimately one of the hottest things I've ever seen.

jokes.text: Ben's talking-head about Leslie filibustering in roller skates: 'I know this is a dire situation. But I swear to God, this is like a crazy sex fantasy for me.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is now filibustering in roller skates, which is politically dire
jokes.punchline: Ben cannot separate the political crisis from his established skates attraction — his confession is immediate, completely earnest, and appropriately horrified at himself
jokes.explanation: This is the perfect payoff to Ben's earlier skates confession. The comedy comes from the collision of his political concern and his deeply personal attraction — and the fact that he admits it in a talking-head with audible horror at himself. 'I swear to God' as a preamble to this confession is perfect. Strong callback execution.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Where else would I rather be than watching the filibuster?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Your birthday party!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know, but this is important.

jokes.text: Tom climbing onto the skee ball ramp to cheat, with his lookout watching. Gets busted. Tom: 'Hey. You're supposed to be my lookout.' Friend: 'I thought it would be funnier to watch you get busted.'
jokes.setup: Tom needs 40,000 tickets for the bear; decides to cheat at skee ball
jokes.punchline: His appointed lookout deliberately lets him get caught because it's more entertaining — a perfect anti-friendship move
jokes.explanation: A solid physical/character comedy beat. The lookout sabotage is a good subversion — the audience expects the cheating to almost work, but the lookout's honest self-interest is funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: I love the gong. It's so exotic. It's got that whole Asian thing going on. You know, like gongs, and pandas, and... dim sum, and... karate, and... fireworks, and... those little dogs with the smushed faces.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Hey, you're a doctor. You know snitches get stitches.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just been busted cheating at skee ball
jokes.punchline: Tom invokes street code ('snitches get stitches') to a doctor, connecting medical stitches to the threat — the medical context makes it unintentionally literal
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient joke that works on the doctor/stitches double meaning. Tom's complete comfort using street code in all situations is character-specific. The literalness of the threat when directed at a surgeon adds a nice layer.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: How much for an extra life?

dialogue.speaker: Arcade Worker
dialogue.line: Five bucks.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Here's twenty. Make it disappear.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Bonderman
dialogue.line: Excuse me, what's going on here?

jokes.text: Leslie's filibuster about her first vote: 'I was in my bedroom, and I was five. I voted for Mildred, my stuffed pig. But my cat, Pancakes, won. She had more funding. Politics, right?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is filibustering and needs to keep talking; she discusses voting
jokes.punchline: Her childhood bedroom 'election' is described with complete political seriousness — the cat winning due to 'more funding' treats stuffed animal democracy as a legitimate parallel
jokes.explanation: 'She had more funding. Politics, right?' is an exceptional Leslie line. It applies real political analysis to a childhood stuffed animal vote in her bedroom, and the weary 'Politics, right?' sounds exactly like a veteran political operative. Near-perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what's romantic? We can look at the same moon tonight. Like, right now, you're looking at the moon, and I'm looking at the same moon.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's... that's literally how the moon works.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, technically we can't see the exact same moon because of the curvature of the Earth and our different positions, so it's actually more of a metaphorical moon.

jokes.text: Leslie asks how long she's been talking. Ben says 'eight minutes.' Leslie considers yielding. Ben: 'Milton doesn't have a lot of time left on Earth.' [to the elderly councilman]. Then immediately: 'Hey, just kidding, bud.'
jokes.setup: Ben is considering Leslie's filibuster; the elderly councilman Milton is present
jokes.punchline: Ben weaponizes Milton's old age as a reason to table the session, then immediately softens it with 'just kidding, bud' — which doesn't make it less dark
jokes.explanation: A good dark joke softened by Ben's immediate backpedal. The 'just kidding, bud' is a nice touch — it's both an attempt to undo the cruelty and evidence that he meant it. Ben's practical pragmatism in a dark direction is a little surprising and gets a laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I used this bear to practice kissing while fantasizing about a Cosby Show character.

jokes.text: Ben's talking-head: 'This is literally the most exciting thing that I have ever seen.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is filibustering in roller skates on his birthday
jokes.punchline: Ben's genuine enthusiasm for a parliamentary procedure crisis — on his birthday, at what should be his party — is delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Ben's nerd enthusiasm for political process is extremely character-specific — the fact that this is his birthday makes it funnier. He's having the best birthday possible, and it's a government filibuster.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey, I've got some consolation prizes for you.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.line: Those are garbage.

jokes.text: Ben: 'I mean, think about it. Where else on earth would you rather spend your birthday with Leslie?' Beat. 'Well, maybe the birthday party she's throwing for me right now.'
jokes.setup: Ben is enthusiastically endorsing the filibuster as an ideal birthday experience
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts his own enthusiasm by remembering there is a literal birthday party happening right now that they're missing
jokes.explanation: A solid self-correcting joke. Ben's immediate reversal lands because it's unexpected — the setup invites agreement, then pulls the rug. Good economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I don't know anything about Rwanda.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But I'm guessing it's a planet.

jokes.text: Leslie removes her roller skates to rest during the filibuster, triggering a gong: 'Bam. Strike one. No sitting.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is struggling with her skates; she briefly takes them off
jokes.punchline: Jamm has apparently set up a gong system with a strike counter, treating the filibuster rules enforcement as a sporting event with a sound effect
jokes.explanation: The gong is a great visual — Jamm has turned the filibuster into a game show. The 'Bam' delivery is very Jamm. Sets up subsequent gong strikes as a running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: We should go night hunting. It's illegal, but that's what makes it fun.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Ron, don't you need a hunting license?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A license is just the government's way of controlling what I do. I don't recognize their authority.

jokes.text: Someone asks if the gong is necessary. Jamm: 'Yes, it is. I love Chinese crap. Lucy Liu, Nintendo, Gangnam Style, sushi, et cetera, et cetera.'
jokes.setup: The appropriateness of the gong is questioned
jokes.punchline: Jamm defends it with a list of 'Chinese crap' that includes Korean pop music (Gangnam Style), Japanese video games (Nintendo), and Japanese food (sushi) — his complete ignorance of Asian cultures is the joke
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Jamm's ignorance is total and shameless — he's lumped four different Asian cultures under 'Chinese' with complete confidence. The list-with-escalation structure and 'et cetera, et cetera' button is a good Jamm delivery. The cringe is intentional and earned.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: As Ronald Reagan once said, 'I don't know what you're talking about, Mommy.'

jokes.text: Tom negotiates to buy the arcade bear for $50 directly. Employee agrees: 'Yeah. Just don't tell my boss.' Boss immediately appears: 'What are you doing, Morris? Tuck in your shirt. God.'
jokes.setup: Tom negotiates a back-channel bear purchase from the arcade employee
jokes.punchline: The employee agrees, immediately followed by his boss appearing — but the boss is only concerned about the untucked shirt, oblivious to the transaction
jokes.explanation: A well-structured misdirection: the audience expects the transaction to get busted, but the boss is focused on something completely irrelevant. The 'Tuck in your shirt. God.' is a great button — the boss is a petty tyrant about minor violations while missing the actual infraction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's so hot in here! The air conditioning is broken.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what this is? This is just like voter suppression. Some people are trying to keep others from voting by making it uncomfortable, and now some people are trying to keep us from being comfortable by breaking the AC. It's the same thing!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to fight back. We need to organize. We need to make sure everyone has the right to air conditioning!

jokes.text: Ron, now apparently very bad at the arcade game, is told by Donna: 'Wow, you suck at this.' Ron: 'Donna, please back up two paces so I can physically destroy this machine.'
jokes.setup: Ron is continuing to fail at the arcade hunting game
jokes.punchline: Ron's response to continued failure is to threaten to physically destroy the machine — the formality of 'please back up two paces' before the threat is perfectly Ron
jokes.explanation: 'Please back up two paces so I can physically destroy this machine' is an exceptional Ron line. The courteous formal request paired with the intent to commit property destruction is quintessential Ron Swanson — polite, deliberate, and absolutely serious. High quotability. The 'two paces' precision is the key comedic detail.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And another thing - we need more funding for the Parks Department, and frankly, I think cake could be part of that solution.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Of course you think cake could solve this. You think cake could solve everything.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not fair.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Last week you suggested we solve the pothole problem with waffles.

jokes.text: Donna: 'Can you chill a little, man? It's not real hunting. It's just a game. That you happen to suck at.'
jokes.setup: Ron is threatening to destroy the arcade machine
jokes.punchline: Donna delivers a reasonable de-escalation ('it's just a game') and then immediately and unnecessarily reinserts the insult ('that you happen to suck at')
jokes.explanation: Donna's comedic rhythm is on display here — she starts sensibly and undercuts herself by adding the jab at the end, seemingly unable to resist. The structure of 'de-escalation + unnecessary burn' is classic Donna.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Democracy is like a cake, you know? It's layered, it's complex, and everyone gets a slice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But honestly, I'm not really thinking about democracy right now. I'm thinking about cake. Do we have cake? I want cake.

jokes.text: Ron considers Donna's 'not real hunting' point: 'You know what? That's a good point.' Donna: 'What? That you suck at this?' Ron: 'That it's not real hunting. Come with me.'
jokes.setup: Donna tells Ron it's not real hunting
jokes.punchline: Donna assumes Ron is agreeing he sucks; Ron clarifies he's agreeing about the unreality — he's going to find ACTUAL hunting
jokes.explanation: A nice beat that sets up whatever Ron is about to do. The misdirection of which 'good point' he's agreeing with is well-structured and tells us something about Ron — he's not acknowledging incompetence, he's identifying an actual deficiency in the game. Very Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Our first mayor, Zachary Timberlake, once said, 'Every citizen has the right to vote, and every Native American has the right to be systematically eradicated.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I really hope that second part is outdated.

jokes.text: Andy to April: 'Just remember. Every time you look up at the moon, I too, will be looking at a moon. Not the same moon, obviously. That's impossible.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April say goodbye before he goes back to London
jokes.punchline: Andy delivers a sweet romantic cliché about the moon, then immediately corrects himself because he genuinely believes they'd be looking at different moons
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The setup is a genuine romantic moment — Andy is trying to say something beautiful — and the punchline ('Not the same moon, obviously. That's impossible.') reveals that he doesn't understand basic astronomy and is CORRECTING himself out of scientific integrity. The joke is funny, sweet, and completely perfect for Andy's character. The correction comes from a place of sincere earnestness, not stupidity-for-laughs. Highly quotable, strong rewatch value, exceptional character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I jumped in.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No reason. Just felt like it.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head: 'I'm proud of Andy. This is the first time he's really gone out on a limb. I knew if he found something that he actually liked doing, he'd be happy.' Then she starts to cry mid-sentence.
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers a heartfelt talking-head about Andy's growth
jokes.punchline: She breaks down crying mid-compliment, unable to hold it together — the sincerity overwhelms her
jokes.explanation: Leslie's emotional overflow is very in-character — she cares deeply about everyone in her office. The comedy comes from the abruptness of the break. It's a warm laugh rather than a big one, but it's real.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, if that's how you feel, I'm going to have to formally revoke the hug we shared earlier.

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head: 'When I was a kid, I taught myself how to make out on this bear. I pretended it was Cockroach from The Cosby Show.'
jokes.setup: Tom recognizes the bear from Ann's purchase — it's the same bear he had as a child
jokes.punchline: His childhood make-out practice partner was a stuffed bear that he imagined as a supporting character from The Cosby Show — specific and deeply strange
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Cockroach from The Cosby Show' is what makes this joke work. Not just any character — Cockroach, a relatively minor character. Tom's childhood romantic imagination is both precocious and absurd. This level of specificity is what separates a good joke from a great character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Civil rights heroes like Rosa Parks, Martin Luther King Jr., and Jennifer Aniston from the Brad Pitt divorce.

jokes.text: April, also wanting the bear: 'Why does Blossom have my bear?' (April is dressed as Blossom.)
jokes.setup: Multiple people want the arcade bear; April arrives costumed
jokes.punchline: April refers to herself in the third person as 'Blossom,' confirming she's in a '90s TV character costume and has staked a claim on the bear
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient joke — April is dressed as Blossom, and referring to herself by costume name rather than her own is a nice touch. The visual gag of the Blossom costume and the escalating bear dispute work together.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm under a lot of pressure at work. My boss wants me to do more, my coworkers expect things from me, and I'm just trying to keep it together.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Like, I was just sitting in the break room, minding my own business, and someone walked in and was like, 'Andy, that's not a toilet.'

jokes.text: Ann explains the bear situation: 'But apparently, he was trying to win it for you. So, I'm sorry. I still have some tickets, though. I can get you a Ninja Turtle balloon, or Cliffhanger on VHS.'
jokes.setup: Ann bought the bear but feels guilty that Tom was trying to win it for Nadia
jokes.punchline: Her consolation prizes are 'a Ninja Turtle balloon or Cliffhanger on VHS' — both items so period-specific and worthless as romantic gestures that they're perfect comedy
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Cliffhanger on VHS' as an alternative gift is excellent — it's a '90s action movie on an obsolete format, offered sincerely as a romantic going-away present. Nadia's response ('That's so sweet, but you're basically offering me garbage') is the perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm like Chuck Norris.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Chuck Norris is now a scared, confused has-been.

jokes.text: Nadia's response to Ann's consolation prizes: 'Aw. That's so sweet, but you're basically offering me garbage.'
jokes.setup: Ann offers Nadia a Ninja Turtle balloon or Cliffhanger on VHS as consolation
jokes.punchline: Nadia's polite acknowledgment followed by 'you're basically offering me garbage' is devastatingly accurate and delivered without malice
jokes.explanation: A perfect button on the consolation prizes joke. 'You're basically offering me garbage' is said warmly and matter-of-factly, making it funnier than if it were delivered as an insult. Highly economical.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I just destroy all the important documents when I get bored. Like, last week I threw out all the permits from 1987.

jokes.text: Nadia: 'Aw. That's so sweet, but you're basically offering me garbage.'
jokes.setup: Ben offers a Ninja Turtle balloon and Cliffhanger on VHS as compensation
jokes.punchline: Nadia delivers the assessment with maximum economy: 'you're basically offering me garbage'
jokes.explanation: The 'Aw. That's so sweet, but...' setup followed by 'you're basically offering me garbage' is a clean punchline. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're gonna do great. Everyone else is just way worse than you.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Like, significantly worse. It's actually impressive how much worse they are.

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head about Nadia going to Rwanda: 'And if I know anything about Rwanda... And I don't. I bet it's full of rich guys who will buy her whatever she wants.'
jokes.setup: Tom is worried Nadia will forget him while she's in Rwanda with Doctors Without Borders
jokes.punchline: He disclaims any knowledge of Rwanda, then immediately delivers a completely wrong characterization of it — imagining it as a playground for wealthy suitors
jokes.explanation: The structure is near-perfect: Tom self-deprecatingly disclaims knowledge of Rwanda, then immediately demonstrates that ignorance by assuming it's Monaco. 'And I don't' as a parenthetical is the key word that makes the subsequent characterization land harder. Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I want democracy.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: What do you really want?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The margarita.

jokes.text: Ron and Donna are now apparently in an outdoor area doing real hunting. Ron: 'Hang on. Do you have a license to hunt at night? Because you need a license.' [Donna reacts.] Ron: 'I thought you were serious. Come on, now. You know I don't give a...'
jokes.setup: Ron has brought Donna to actual night hunting, apparently
jokes.punchline: Ron questions Donna about her hunting license — Donna clearly doesn't have one — but Ron reveals he's joking about caring: 'You know I don't give a...'
jokes.explanation: Ron's 'I don't give a [expletive] about licensing' being played as a punchline works because the setup creates genuine tension — Ron is a lawful person about hunting — and then reveals he also genuinely does not care about night hunting laws.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Ron, why are you covered in blood?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's not human blood.

jokes.text: Leslie's filibuster speech: 'As Ronald Reagan would say, "Well, Mommy, I believe voting rights are important."'
jokes.setup: Leslie is padding her filibuster with political references
jokes.punchline: The Reagan impression/quote is patently made up — Reagan called Nancy 'Mommy' but the quote itself is Leslie inventing what Reagan would say about voting rights, filtered through his pet name
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Leslie is obviously making up the quote, and the 'Mommy' detail is an accurate Reagan/Nancy reference that makes it specific. It also reflects Leslie's exhaustion starting to show in her increasingly creative citations.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: How do you even get women to date you?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's simple. Love and hate are very similar emotions. So I tell women that I hate them.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: They think I'm using some kind of fake psychology, but really I just hate them.

jokes.text: Leslie during the filibuster: 'Does anyone else think it's hot in here? These overalls are really starchy.' Jamm: 'Oh, yeah, maybe that's because I turned up the heat to 90 and, oh, the knob broke off in my hand. Oops.'
jokes.setup: Leslie mentions it's hot in the council chambers
jokes.punchline: Jamm immediately reveals he turned the heat to 90 to sabotage her filibuster, then performs 'accidental' regret with zero commitment
jokes.explanation: Jamm's 'Oops' after confessing to a clear deliberate act of sabotage is perfectly delivered. The 'oh, the knob broke off in my hand' feigning accident is classic Jamm villainy — he doesn't even try to be convincing.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Thanks for the advice, kid.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Did you just call me 'kid'?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, because you're giving me relationship advice when you clearly still have feelings for me.

jokes.text: Leslie (filibustering): 'the local city councilwoman, who is starving and thinking about her husband's Reservoir Dogs themed birthday cake and wanting to eat it really badly.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to maintain her filibuster speech about voting rights while increasingly desperate
jokes.punchline: She slips into third-person monologue about herself — revealing her distraction to the very audience she's addressing
jokes.explanation: Leslie's filibuster deteriorating into third-person self-pity is great character comedy. The 'Reservoir Dogs themed birthday cake' detail is specific and funny — this is very Ben.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What is this?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A bologna sandwich for your trip!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You used cookies as bread.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, they're chocolate chip! I thought it'd be a fun surprise.

jokes.text: Leslie, fading from hunger, starts conflating voting rights with food: 'Democracy is not unlike a cake. It's layered, delicious, chocolate, and I want some.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is starving; Ben notes she's thinking about her husband's birthday cake
jokes.punchline: Leslie's food obsession takes over her political rhetoric — her democracy metaphor is completely coherent as a cake description and completely incoherent as a political statement
jokes.explanation: This is a great Leslie joke. She genuinely believes in democracy AND in food, and the two have become indistinguishable in her exhaustion. 'It's layered, delicious, chocolate, and I want some' works perfectly as both a democracy metaphor and a literal cake desire. Very high character integration — this is a Leslie Knope joke and nobody else's.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you're doing that thing where you're bouncing around like Charlie Brown doing the happy dance.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Once she starts thinking about birthday cake, she's basically useless until she eats birthday cake.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has started talking about birthday cake during the filibuster
jokes.punchline: Ben delivers a matter-of-fact diagnostic about Leslie's food-motivation as if it's a well-established clinical condition
jokes.explanation: Ben speaks about Leslie's food obsession with the weary expertise of a long-married man who has mapped her weaknesses. The framing as clinical fact ('basically useless until she eats birthday cake') is funny because it's clearly accurate.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Oh, does little Leslie need to find a potty? Does somebody need a nappy change?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: You know what, Jeremy? I don't have time for your childish games.

jokes.text: Leslie's filibuster speech: 'It was the first mayor of Pawnee in 1817 who said, "All we have is the right to vote. And the right to kill Indians without consequence." And I believe that half of that statement is still true today.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is citing historical Pawnee statements in support of voting rights
jokes.punchline: The historical quote is horrific; Leslie validates only the voting rights half — but the very existence of the Pawnee founding quote as a real document, and Leslie's need to carefully specify WHICH half she endorses, is the joke
jokes.explanation: A superb dark/satirical joke that requires one beat to land. The horror of the historical quote is undercut by Leslie's cheerful pivot — 'And I believe that half of that statement is still true today' — which is both funny and a sharp political satire. The specificity ('in 1817') and the formal citation structure make it feel authentic to Pawnee's history. One of the episode's strongest.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, my hair looks amazing right now. I can't mess it up.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So your hair is more important than hugging me?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes. Obviously.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: *hurt look*

jokes.text: Andy is found hiding in a dumpster. He claims: 'I was just here in this dumpster, because I jumped in.' April: 'Get out.' Ron: 'We need to talk. About what? Fresh air. Real weapons. An honest kill.'
jokes.setup: Ron is looking for Andy, apparently to take him real hunting
jokes.punchline: Andy is inexplicably in a dumpster; his explanation ('I jumped in') is not an explanation at all. Ron's invitation — 'Fresh air. Real weapons. An honest kill.' — is delivered as if he's narrating a perfume commercial
jokes.explanation: Andy in a dumpster with no coherent explanation is very Andy. Ron's three-word recruitment pitch ('Fresh air. Real weapons. An honest kill.') is poetic in Ron's worldview. The combination works as a character collision.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We stole the bear like you said, Ann.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? I never said to steal it!

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.line: We took it to the pawn shop to get our money back.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: They gave us eight dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Eight dollars? For a forty-thousand-dollar bear?

jokes.text: Ron decides going hunting is a good idea, heads out, then immediately turns back: 'You want to go back and play that video game, don't you?' Ron (defeated): 'Yes. Damn it.'
jokes.setup: Ron has dramatically recruited Andy for real hunting
jokes.punchline: Donna calls him on it immediately — Ron actually wants to go back and beat the arcade game — and he folds instantly with 'Yes. Damn it.'
jokes.explanation: A perfect payoff to the entire Ron/arcade game arc. The reveal that Ron's 'real hunting' plan was actually about getting a rematch on the video game, combined with the immediate deflation of 'Yes. Damn it.' — Ron can't even sustain the lie. This is Ron being human beneath the stoic exterior. Very strong callback execution.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not entering my initials. That's private.

jokes.text: The Eagletonians reveal they came to support their OWN voting rights but will NOT vote for Leslie. Leslie: 'Sir, I formally revoke our hug.' Eagletonian: 'Well, you can't. It happened.'
jokes.setup: Leslie hugged an Eagletonian in gratitude, only to learn they plan to vote against her
jokes.punchline: Leslie attempts to formally revoke the hug; the Eagletonian refuses on the grounds that it already occurred — the hug is legally binding
jokes.explanation: A delightful bit of Leslie-specific comedy — she uses formal parliamentary language ('I formally revoke') for a hug, and the Eagletonian counters with equally formal irrevocability. The idea that hugs are contractual and irreversible is very funny, and the exchange is brief and well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I was in the bathroom this morning, and I realized I've been using the same loofah for three years. THREE YEARS. So I decided to throw it away and get a new one, which is very responsible, very adult of me—

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: Leslie, why are you telling me this?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not! I mean, I wasn't planning to. I was just... thinking out loud. About loofahs. Which is a normal thing to think about. Everyone thinks about loofahs.

jokes.text: Eagletonian: 'We stand on the side of Rosa Parks. And Gandhi. And Team Aniston.'
jokes.setup: The Eagletonians are invoking civil rights heroes to justify their voting rights position
jokes.punchline: The list of moral exemplars escalates from Rosa Parks to Gandhi and then collapses into 'Team Aniston' — the Jennifer Aniston/Brad Pitt divorce taking celebrity gossip
jokes.explanation: The joke structure here is near-perfect. Rosa Parks → Gandhi → Team Aniston is a three-part list that escalates then catastrophically deflates with a tabloid celebrity gossip reference. The formal 'We stand on the side of' makes the 'Team Aniston' landing even more absurd. Economy is excellent. One of the episode's best joke structures.

dialogue.speaker: Ingrid
dialogue.line: I'm thanking you for the filibuster. The political act, not the bathroom experience.

jokes.text: Eagletonian: 'One small vote for Pawnee is one giant leap of voting for mankind.'
jokes.setup: Eagletonians continue their grandiose civil rights framing
jokes.punchline: A mangled Neil Armstrong quote — 'one small step' becomes 'one small vote' and 'one giant leap for mankind' becomes 'one giant leap of voting for mankind' — clunkily inserted
jokes.explanation: A functional quote-mangle joke that gets a mild chuckle. The 'leap of voting for mankind' phrasing is awkward in a deliberate way. Weaker than the 'Team Aniston' line that preceded it, but they serve as a pair establishing Eagletonian pomposity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We should put roller skates back on.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I... that's... wow.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Nothing, I just... roller skates.

jokes.text: Jamm tries to mess with Leslie; Ben: 'Hey, man. Leave my gong alone. The reverb is the best part.'
jokes.setup: Jamm is interfering with the gong system he himself installed
jokes.punchline: Ben has become so invested in the filibuster that he's now defending the gong that Jamm set up to penalize his wife
jokes.explanation: Ben's enthusiasm for the filibuster as spectacle has led him to defend Jamm's hostile tool on aesthetic grounds. 'The reverb is the best part' is very specific and funny — Ben has opinions about this gong's audio quality.

jokes.text: Leslie pauses in her filibuster as Eagletonians start chanting 'Eagleton! Eagleton!' in the gallery — for a recall vote that might replace her.
jokes.setup: Leslie is fighting to preserve Eagletonians' voting rights
jokes.punchline: The crowd she's protecting chants for Eagleton — not for Leslie — as she fights for their right to vote against her
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony here is the comedy — Leslie is filibustering to protect the rights of people who are currently chanting against her. It's the episode's central comic premise crystallized in a moment.

jokes.text: Leslie has a moment of clarity, starts to reason herself into yielding, gets close — then: 'No one prevents people in my town from voting. Not on my watch. The filibuster is on.'
jokes.setup: Leslie logically figures out that it might benefit her to let Jamm's bill pass so Eagletonians can't vote against her
jokes.punchline: Her principles override her self-interest — and the fact that she makes the selfless choice while fully aware it might end her career is played straight but underscored with the comedy of inevitability (everyone in the audience knew she would)
jokes.explanation: More character moment than pure joke, but the comedy comes from Leslie's earnestness and the predictability that makes it both funny and warm. The audience always knew she'd do this.

jokes.text: Andy's confessional: 'I can't go back to London. I'm totally in over my head on this project. Every day, someone comes up to me and says, "I need your approval on this, Mr. Dwyer. I need your signature, Mr. Dwyer. That's not a toilet, Mr. Dwyer."'
jokes.setup: Andy admitted he told April everything was going great in London
jokes.punchline: The list of workplace demands escalates from normal to 'That's not a toilet, Mr. Dwyer' — implying Andy has been using something inappropriate as a bathroom
jokes.explanation: A brilliant escalation joke. The list format lulls you into expecting bureaucratic complaints, then delivers 'That's not a toilet, Mr. Dwyer' — which implies something spectacular and unspecified has gone wrong. The 'Mr. Dwyer' formality makes Andy's chaos funnier because he's being addressed with respect while apparently urinating on something in an office building. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Andy updates his Chuck Norris metaphor: 'I am. But I'm like Chuck Norris now. Some old guy with a beard who used to be good at karate, but became a dumb has-been, and is scared and confused about his big London job.'
jokes.setup: April reminds Andy he compared himself to Chuck Norris earlier
jokes.punchline: Andy revises the metaphor to current Chuck Norris — a confused, bearded has-been — which is both accurate and a pitch-perfect summary of his own feelings, delivered with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: A superb callback execution. Andy updates his own metaphor accurately — 'scared and confused about his big London job' is the key detail, applied to both present-day Chuck Norris and himself simultaneously. The joke works on multiple levels and has high quotability.

jokes.text: April's workplace confession: 'I don't know how to run an Animal Control department. Half the documents I get, I put right into the shredder because they're so boring.'
jokes.setup: April is telling Andy that nobody knows what they're doing at work
jokes.punchline: April's contribution to the universal 'faking it' thesis is that she shreds documents because they're boring — a genuinely alarming Animal Control administrative revelation
jokes.explanation: April's confession is both encouraging (everyone fakes it) and genuinely alarming (she's in charge of animal control and shreds paperwork for being boring). The 'because they're so boring' justification is perfectly April — she's not incompetent, she's indifferent, which is somehow worse and funnier.

jokes.text: April's pep talk conclusion: 'Deep down, everyone is just faking it until they figure it out. And you will, too. Because you are awesome and everyone else sucks.'
jokes.setup: April is delivering a genuine, encouraging speech to Andy
jokes.punchline: The speech starts sincerely and ends with 'everyone else sucks' — April's version of a pep talk inevitably swerves into misanthropy, which is her love language
jokes.explanation: 'Because you are awesome and everyone else sucks' is an extremely quotable April line. It's completely character-specific — her affection expressed as comparative dismissal of everyone else is April's emotional register. The economy is near-perfect: it's one sentence that captures her whole character.

jokes.text: Jamm offers Leslie a margarita while she's filibustering, taunting her with it: 'Mmm-mmm-mmm! How I know you would love an ice-cold frozen marg.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is dying of heat in a 90-degree council chamber, dehydrated, hungry
jokes.punchline: Jamm taunts her with a margarita — an extremely specific and petty form of torture — in a sing-song voice
jokes.explanation: The margarita temptation sequence works as Jamm torture comedy — he's perfectly villain-ish in a petty, small-stakes way. The 'Mmm-mmm-mmm' is a good Jamm sound effect.

jokes.text: Ron emerges from somewhere covered in blood. Worker: 'Why are you covered in blood?' Ron: 'Don't worry. It's not human.' Then, looking at destroyed arcade game: 'I hope you've made peace with your God, small electronic deer.'
jokes.setup: Ron went to do real hunting after the arcade game failure
jokes.punchline: Ron returns covered in blood — 'Don't worry, it's not human' — and then eulogizes the arcade game deer he's about to destroy with formal respect
jokes.explanation: 'Don't worry. It's not human.' followed by 'I hope you've made peace with your God, small electronic deer.' — this might be the episode's best joke sequence. The first line reassures with unexpected understatement (his need to specify 'not human' implies the blood is real and abundant). The eulogy for the arcade game deer is Ron at his absolute peak: hunting solemnity applied to a pixelated target, delivered with total sincerity. 'Small electronic deer' is a perfect noun phrase. Exceptional character integration, economy, and originality.

jokes.text: Ron enters the party covered in blood: 'Excuse me, worker. Bring me a bucket of beers and four hot dogs, please and thank you.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Donna have been 'hunting' outside; Ron returns to the party
jokes.punchline: Ron returns covered in blood and calmly orders food with perfect politeness — the gore plus the courtesy creates the comedy
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the Ron/Donna hunting subplot is perfectly executed. The visual of Ron covered in blood casually ordering beers and hot dogs with a 'please and thank you' is pure Ron Swanson energy. The callback lands hard because we've been waiting to see what happened. One of the episode's best visual comedy moments.

jokes.text: Ann persuades Tom to forget the bear: 'Tom, bear or no bear, she clearly likes you. Actually, how do you even get girls like her or me to go out with you?'
jokes.setup: Ann is giving Tom advice about Nadia
jokes.punchline: Ann's sincere endorsement of Tom ('she clearly likes you') pivots immediately into insulting him ('how do you even get girls like her or me to go out with you?')
jokes.explanation: Ann's backhanded relationship advice is a consistent source of comedy — she can't help herself. The pivot from encouragement to confusion about Tom's appeal is well-timed.

jokes.text: Tom's response to how he gets women: 'Scientists say the emotions of love and hate are very close to each other. That's what I tell women.'
jokes.setup: Ann asks how Tom gets attractive women to go out with him
jokes.punchline: Tom's seduction technique is citing fake science to confuse women into dating him — the 'That's what I tell women' framing implies this is a rehearsed line he deploys
jokes.explanation: A very Tom joke. The pseudo-science framing with 'Scientists say' followed by 'That's what I tell women' reveals a fully developed — and baffling — seduction strategy. It's specific to Tom in a way that's both funny and somehow believable. High character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: Tom concludes with: 'I know conversations like this are hard for you because you still have feelings for me. But you'll land on your feet, kid. Run or I punch you. No punchies!'
jokes.setup: Ann has been giving Tom good advice about Nadia
jokes.punchline: Tom dismisses her help as evidence of her lingering feelings for him, then tells her she'll be fine — completely inverting the power dynamic — and then issues a non-threat of 'No punchies!' when she threatens him
jokes.explanation: Tom's inversion of the advisor/advisee dynamic — suddenly he's the one comforting Ann about her feelings — is very Tom. 'No punchies!' is a solid button that works as physical comedy implies Ann has raised her fist.

jokes.text: Andy and April's goodbye: April produces five bologna sandwiches on cookies. 'I made you five bologna sandwiches in case you get hungry on the way to the airport.' 'Did you...?' 'Yes, I used cookies instead of bread.'
jokes.setup: April says goodbye to Andy before he returns to London
jokes.punchline: April has made goodbye sandwiches — which is sweet — but with cookies instead of bread, which is characteristically, lovably wrong
jokes.explanation: The cookie-bread sandwiches are a perfect April detail. They're simultaneously sweet (she thought of it) and wrong (cookies instead of bread). The 'Did you—?' / 'Yes, I used cookies instead of bread' exchange is perfectly economical. Very high character integration — this is exactly how April would make sandwiches.

jokes.text: Andy inexplicably finds his wallet in a dumpster: 'Ha-ha! Found it. I got it. I left my wallet in here earlier, I guess. Whoo! All good now.'
jokes.setup: Andy is back at the dumpster from earlier in the episode
jokes.punchline: Andy was apparently in the dumpster earlier NOT to hide, but because he left his wallet in it — which is simultaneously a callback and a revelation that his earlier explanation ('I jumped in') was even more absurd than understood
jokes.explanation: A great retroactive punchline. Andy was in the dumpster because he lost his wallet in it — a completely realistic Andy explanation — which makes his earlier 'I jumped in' cover story inexplicably worse than the truth. 'All good now' delivered with total satisfaction is perfect Andy.

jokes.text: Ben reads the city charter trying to find Leslie a bathroom break option: 'She's dancing around like she's a character in one of those Peanuts cartoons.'
jokes.setup: Leslie desperately needs a bathroom break but the rules don't allow it
jokes.punchline: Ben's visual description of Leslie's desperate dance as a Peanuts cartoon character is both accurate and affectionate
jokes.explanation: The Peanuts comparison is oddly specific and very accurate — the Peanuts pee-pee dance is a recognizable cultural reference. Ben's delivery would be entirely affectionate, which adds warmth to the joke.

jokes.text: Jamm taunts Leslie in baby talk: 'Hey, Knope, how you feeling over there? You need to go pee-pee? Pee-pee times? Make wee-wee?' Then Leslie's countdown: 'Five more seconds. Four! Three! Two! One!'
jokes.setup: Leslie is seconds from the session ending, visibly desperate
jokes.punchline: Jamm's baby-talk taunting ('pee-pee times', 'wee-wee') is petty and cringe-inducing; Leslie's count with escalating urgency is the payoff
jokes.explanation: Jamm's baby talk is the kind of cartoonish villainy the show deploys well. The countdown creates genuine tension and then releases it cleanly. Leslie's counting is the real beat — the physical desperation selling the joke.

jokes.text: Session is adjourned. Leslie, running: 'Yes! You were amazing.' Ben: 'I love you, but move. I have to go to the whizz palace.'
jokes.setup: The filibuster succeeds; Ben moves to hug Leslie
jokes.punchline: Leslie interrupts Ben's celebration with 'I love you, but move' — romantic pragmatism — then 'I have to go to the whizz palace' replaces 'bathroom' with a very Leslie noun
jokes.explanation: 'I have to go to the whizz palace' is a great line — 'palace' is an unexpectedly grandiose noun for a public restroom, delivered with complete earnestness by someone who desperately needs to use it.

jokes.text: Leslie, running past everyone, stops briefly to fix her hair in a mirror. Ben: 'She didn't have time to hug me, but she could do that?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is running to the bathroom at maximum urgency
jokes.punchline: Despite her emergency, Leslie cannot pass a mirror without addressing her appearance — she pauses her desperate sprint to fix her hair
jokes.explanation: A perfect visual gag that requires no explanation. Leslie's vanity overrides even a bladder emergency. Ben's bewildered 'She didn't have time to hug me, but she could do that?' is the ideal reaction beat.

jokes.text: Tom and Nadia steal the bear from Ann. Tom: 'This is on you. You told us to make a memory.' Ann: 'There's your money back.' Nadia: 'Let go!' Ann: 'Suck it!'
jokes.setup: Ann advised Tom to make a memorable moment with Nadia; they take her at her word
jokes.punchline: Tom and Nadia steal the bear from Ann, citing Ann's own advice as justification — 'This is on you' — while Ann yells 'Suck it!' as they escape
jokes.explanation: The bear arc pays off with physical comedy and a great 'Suck it!' button from Ann. 'This is on you. You told us to make a memory.' is a great Tom deflection that's technically correct. The ensemble energy makes this sequence work.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Together, we truly did steal a toy from your pregnant friend.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Nadia have just stolen the bear from Ann
jokes.punchline: Tom's triumphant summary focuses on the most unflattering possible framing — 'steal a toy from your pregnant friend' — delivered as if it's a proud accomplishment
jokes.explanation: Tom's complete lack of shame is on full display. 'We truly did steal a toy from your pregnant friend' is the exact worst-case framing of what they did, delivered as a victory recap. The word 'truly' elevates it — Tom is not just noting what happened, he's affirming it. Highly quotable and perfectly economical.

jokes.text: Tom asks if Nadia will call him when she returns from Rwanda. Nadia: 'Ugh! Clingy.' Tom: 'Oh, no. Sorry.' Nadia: 'No, no, no. I'm kidding. Of course I'll call you when I come back.'
jokes.setup: Tom cautiously asks if they can continue seeing each other when she returns
jokes.punchline: Nadia's 'Ugh! Clingy' appears to be a rejection, then immediately reverses — she was joking, she'll call
jokes.explanation: A functional misdirection beat. The setup/fake-out works but the stakes are low and it's a predictable structure. Gets a warm laugh as a romantic payoff rather than a comedy beat.

jokes.text: Ron successfully beats the arcade hunting game: 'Now, that's what I call shooting. That's a new record. Hey, look at that. You finally made it into the top ten. Now, you can enter your initials.' Ron: 'My initials are private.'
jokes.setup: Ron has finally beaten the arcade deer-hunting game
jokes.punchline: Ron refuses to enter his initials on the high score board, treating his personal initials as classified information
jokes.explanation: 'My initials are private.' is a superb Ron Swanson line. It's the perfect capstone to the entire arcade game storyline — he's beaten the machine, earned his place in the top ten, and then refuses to mark it. His privacy paranoia extends even to a children's arcade game high score board. Very high character integration, quotability, and a satisfying arc payoff.

jokes.text: Leslie's post-filibuster monologue to the camera, then: 'Oh, my God. That was epic. I was peeing so freaking hard, it was like a Jacuzzi jet or...' Notices Ingrid: 'Hi, Leslie.' Leslie: 'Hey. Ingrid. I wasn't talking about the velocity of my pee. Because you are a very smart and classy lady.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is talking to Ben about how hard she just urinated after the filibuster
jokes.punchline: She spots Ingrid De Forest — her Eagletonian political opponent — standing nearby mid-description, and immediately tries to walk it back with a compliment
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly structured cringe comedy moment. 'I was peeing so freaking hard, it was like a Jacuzzi jet' is extremely quotable, and the immediate context-switch — discovering your political opponent heard it — followed by 'I wasn't talking about the velocity of my pee. Because you are a very smart and classy lady.' is perfect Leslie: trying to recover social dignity with a compliment that just underscores the problem. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Leslie asks why she'd need roller skates if they're not going to the party. Ben: 'Then, why would you need to put on roller skates?' Leslie: 'Oh, yeah. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah. We're just... Just. Skates.'
jokes.setup: Ben suggests they go home rather than the party; Leslie mentions putting on roller skates
jokes.punchline: Ben's question triggers Leslie's realization that the skates are for a private, at-home reason — her flustered 'Just. Skates.' with the trailing off is the callback payoff to Ben's entire skating attraction
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke and one of the best callbacks in the episode. Leslie's 'Just. Skates.' with the trailing-off ellipsis is the final payoff on Ben's established attraction, confirmed by Leslie's flustered realization she accidentally almost explained their private plans. The structure of 'misdirection → realization → flustered deflection' is perfectly constructed, and 'Just. Skates.' is a brilliant comedic button — three words that imply everything.

tmdb_overview: Leslie prepares a haunted house with Ben, Ann and Chris for Halloween on the day of the recall vote. Meanwhile, Tom fears the end of Rent-A-Swag and persuades Ron to help save his business.
insight: Ben's filibuster delivers 60 jokes in 24 minutes, heavy on cringe absurdism.
